articles.title: Uzbekistan Proposes One-Stop Center for Migrant Workers Heading to Russia - The Times Of Central Asia
articles.summary: Uzbekistan Proposes One-Stop Center for Migrant Workers Heading to Russia  The Times Of Central Asia
articles.full_text:
Uzbekistan has proposed establishing a one-stop center where citizens planning to work in Russia could complete key migration procedures before departure.
The initiative was discussed at a meeting between Uzbekistan Migration Agency Director Muhsinxo‘ja Abdurahmonov and Russian Ambassador to Uzbekistan Alexey Yerkhov.
The Migration Agency also wants Russian-language examinations to be available in the regions so applicants do not have to travel to Tashkent. It said the necessary infrastructure has been prepared in four regions.
Uzbekistan is proposing that citizens travel to Russia for specific vacancies. Prospective workers would know their employer and working conditions in advance.
In 2025, Tashkent and Moscow considered conducting medical examinations and Russian-language tests at branches of Russian universities in Tashkent and Jizzakh.
The latest initiative comes as work-related travel from Uzbekistan to Russia has declined. In January-June 2026, Uzbek citizens made more than 1.1 million entries into Russia declaring work as the purpose of their trip, down 13.2% from a year earlier. Across Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and Kyrgyzstan, work-related entries fell by about 15%, from more than 2.3 million to 1.9 million. The figures count border crossings rather than individual workers, meaning the same person can be counted more than once.
Despite fewer work-related entries into Russia, cross-border remittances to Uzbekistan reached $9.3 billion in the first half of 2026, up 13% year-on-year. The Central Bank attributed the increase to sustained demand for labor and relatively high wages in traditional destination countries for Uzbek migrant workers, as well as the strengthening of national currencies.
The Central Bank also pointed to signs of diversification in the geography of labor migration. Transfers from the United Kingdom increased by 62% year-on-year, those from European Union countries by 27%, and those from the United States by 19%.

articles.title: Tajikistan Begins Receiving Iranian Oil, Testing New Supply Route And Extent Of US Sanctions - Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty
articles.summary: Tajikistan Begins Receiving Iranian Oil, Testing New Supply Route And Extent Of US Sanctions  Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty
articles.full_text:
Tajikistan announced that it is now receiving oil and petroleum products from Iran, opening a potential new energy source for a country whose fuel supplies have long been dominated by Russia.
The deliveries began in late August, Tajikistan's Energy and Water Resources Ministry told the Asia-Plus news agency, following talks between the two countries on expanding cooperation in the oil and gas sector.
The ministry has not disclosed the volume of the shipments, their commercial terms, or how the oil and petroleum products were transported to Tajikistan.
The move also raises questions about potential US secondary sanctions for doing business with Iran, particularly as Washington has stepped up pressure on Tehran's oil revenues.
A US Treasury official, who asked not to be identified, said the department would not comment on specific allegations of sanctions violations but warned that Iran's petroleum and petrochemical sectors are subject to increased sanctions risk.
"Anyone operating in that sector incurs that risk themselves should they continue to choose to do so," the official said in an e-mailed response to RFE/RL.
Tajikistan has asked Iran to supply up to 2.55 million tons of crude oil and petroleum products annually, including gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel. But that figure represents a requested or potential volume rather than the amount currently being delivered.
The potential shift toward Iranian supplies could give Dushanbe another option, although the economics and logistics of moving large quantities of Iranian oil to landlocked Tajikistan remain unclear.
The oil deal comes as Tajikistan faces continued uncertainty over fuel supplies from Russia, which accounted for more than 91 percent of the country's petroleum-product imports in the first half of 2026.
Russian fuel shortages and export restrictions, exacerbated by Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries, have prompted Tajikistan and other Central Asian countries to seek alternative sources.
In July, Tajik authorities said they were in talks with neighboring countries to secure future supplies.
Tajik political analyst Parviz Mullojonov said the search for Iranian supplies was being driven in part by Tajikistan's need to secure alternative energy sources.
Warming Relations
The Iranian deliveries also come amid a broader warming of relations between Dushanbe and Tehran.
"The report that Iran has started to sell oil to Tajikistan comes as the relation between Dushanbe and Tehran is warming and they're becoming closer," said Edward Lemon, president of the Oxus Society for Central Asian Affairs.
Tajikistan and Iran, which share close linguistic and historic ties, established diplomatic relations in 1992. Tajikistan's Foreign Ministry says bilateral trade reached $438 million in 2025, up 28 percent from the previous year, and that the countries have signed more than 200 agreements and memorandums.
At a meeting of the Tajik-Iranian intergovernmental commission in Dushanbe in May, officials discussed energy, transport, industry, investment, science, and technology.
The two countries also have defense ties. In 2022, Iran and Tajikistan inaugurated a drone-manufacturing facility in Dushanbe, designed to produce Iranian-designed Ababil-2 drones.
But relations between the two countries have not always been close. Ties deteriorated sharply in the mid-2010s, with Dushanbe wary of Tehran's alleged support for Tajikistan's banned Islamic Renaissance Party.
In 2017, Dushanbe also accused Tehran of involvement in a series of political killings in Tajikistan in the 1990s, allegations that Tehran denied.
The relationship began to thaw in the early 2020s. In 2022, Tajik President Emomali Rahmon visited Tehran, and the two sides pledged to strengthen diplomatic, trade, and security ties.
The Sanctions Question
A Tajik delegation that visited Tehran in August held talks with Iranian officials responsible for oil products and railways, with energy supplies and logistics among the issues discussed, according to the Tajik Embassy in Tehran.
But closer energy cooperation with Iran could also create complications for Dushanbe as Washington increases pressure on Tehran.
Under US Iran sanctions authorities, foreign companies and financial institutions can face sanctions for certain significant transactions involving Iranian petroleum and petroleum products.
The US Treasury official also emphasized the secondary sanctions exposure for those who continue doing business with the Iranian regime and said any entity facilitating money laundering or sanctions evasion on behalf of Iran risks being cut off from the US financial system.
The Treasury Department has repeatedly warned of sanctions exposure linked to Iranian oil and in August announced an expansion of conduct that could trigger secondary sanctions.
A State Department spokesperson said in an e-mailed response to RFE/RL that the United States would continue to "disrupt, expose, and dismantle" Iranian military and proliferation activities, procurement schemes, malicious cyberoperations, and illicit oil trade that sustain what Washington calls the Iranian regime's "malign behavior."
The spokesperson called on the international community to join the United States in holding those involved accountable.
Lemon said the possibility of secondary sanctions should factor into Dushanbe's calculations as it expands purchases from Iran.
"Tajikistan could of course become one of those countries," he said.
At the same time, Lemon said, the scale of Tajik-Iranian cooperation could be important in determining how seriously Washington views the relationship.
"The scale of cooperation is quite low, much in contrast to countries such as Russia or China," he said.
Mullojonov said Tajikistan was seeking to balance relations with the United States, Russia, China, Turkey, and other powers while pursuing its own economic interests.
"Maintaining a diplomatic balance is incredibly difficult because these global powers often have conflicting agendas," Mullojonov said.
For now, it remains unclear whether Iranian oil can become a substantial alternative to Russian supplies.
RFE/RL contacted Tajikistan's Energy and Foreign Affairs ministries for comment but has not received a response.

articles.title: Russia’s A7 denies Iran links after US sanctions payment network - Iran International
articles.summary: Russia’s A7 denies Iran links after US sanctions payment network  Iran International
articles.full_text:
Russia’s A7 payment platform denied links to Iran on Friday after the United States imposed sanctions on the company and its affiliated network, accusing them of helping Tehran evade sanctions.
“A7 categorically rejects any allegations that it has worked with Iran or terrorist organizations,” the company said in a statement.
It added that it was providing “uninterrupted payment settlements for the Russian market, which has been subjected to unlawful restrictive measures.”
The company said it was servicing “legitimate import and export operations involving consumer goods and commodities.”

articles.title: Oleshky: How Russia Governs Through Humanitarian Decline - Institute for the Study of War
articles.summary: Oleshky: How Russia Governs Through Humanitarian Decline  Institute for the Study of War

source_detail.name: Institute for the Study of War

articles.full_text:
The ongoing humanitarian crisis in the occupied Oleshky area reflects the coercive logic of Russian occupation governance in a heavily damaged frontline city. Oleshky has become a test case for Russian rule in an area marked by depopulation, damaged infrastructure, chronic insecurity, and growing isolation from the rest of Ukraine. Rather than reversing these conditions, Russian occupation authorities appear to govern through them, leveraging residents’ increasing dependence on occupation-controlled services, institutions, and administrative systems to sustain control. As humanitarian vulnerabilities deepen and alternatives to occupation governance diminish, humanitarian decline and Russian occupation rule become mutually reinforcing.
Oleshky is a small town directly on the left (east) bank of the Dnipro River in Ukraine’s southern Kherson Oblast. Oleshky had a pre-war population of around 24,000 people, while around 40,000 people lived in the wider surrounding area of settlements on the left bank of the Dnipro (settlements including Hola Prystan, Stara Zburivka, Nova Zburivka, Kardashynka, Solontsi, Pishchanivka, Kozachi Laheri, and others).[1] Oleshky has become the epicenter of a mounting humanitarian crisis since late 2025, but similarly dire conditions exist in nearby left bank towns and villages.
Russian forces occupied these left bank settlements on February 24, 2022 — the first day of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine — during the initial military push to occupy all of Kherson Oblast from positions in occupied Crimea. Russian troops largely maintained a distance from Oleshky itself in the first few weeks of the invasion, and remaining elements of the Ukrainian city administration attempted to organize self-governance efforts and self-sufficient security patrols while refusing to directly cooperate with Russian soldiers.[2] Geolocated images show Russian forces had officially entered Oleshky as of late March 2022, breaking the tacit governance agreement that had been in place with the remaining Ukrainian officials.[3] Russian forces and occupation officials took full control of Oleshky in late April 2022, however, and about 40 percent of the pre-war population fled to Ukrainian-held territory while security checkpoints were still open.[4]
The occupation of the Oleshky area followed a similar pattern to the violent imposition of Russian rule across Ukraine. Russian forces brutally cracked down against any perceived dissent against the occupation, kidnapping and orchestrating enforced disappearances against prominent local officials or veterans of the Ukrainian military and their families.[5] The Ukrainian General Staff reported that Russian forces blocked evacuation routes and humanitarian corridors in the early stages of the invasion, effectively trapping people in the Oleshky area.[6] Oleshky also faced many of the same demographic engineering tactics that Russia has applied elsewhere in occupied Ukraine, including the resettlement of Russians into the area and the parallel forced removal or deportation of Ukrainians.[7] In one particularly notable instance, Russia forcibly removed 84 disabled adult and minor residents from the Oleshky Specialized Boarding School, relocating the residents to care facilities throughout occupied Ukraine and Russia — a clear example of forced transfer and illegal deportation under international law.[8]
After Ukraine liberated western Kherson Oblast up to the Dnipro River in November 2022, Oleshky and its neighbors became the new Kherson Oblast frontline, firmly under Russia’s grasp and increasingly trapped by their geography. Russian forces dug into positions in and around Oleshky, often co-mingling with civilian residents and basing military equipment in the area.[9] Ukrainian open-source investigative outlet Slidstvo Info reported that units of the 126th Coastal Defense Brigade (Russian Black Sea Fleet) and the 331st Guards Airborne Regiment (98th Airborne [VDV] Division) are likely based in or near Oleshky and may be complicit in various abuses against the civilian population in the area.[10]
Oleshky and other settlements on the Dnipro’s left bank suffered disproportionately because of Russia’s June 6, 2023 destruction of the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant (KHPP) dam.[11] The subsequent flooding nearly submerged the Oleshky area entirely, and Russian forces refused to facilitate evacuation or humanitarian support efforts. Up to 500 residents of Oleshky may have died during the flooding because Russian forces reportedly refused to evacuate anyone without a Russian passport.[12] The flooding of cemeteries throughout the area led to water contamination that created an acute sanitation crisis.[13] Russian occupation officials exploited the flood to consolidate further control over Oleshky’s residents, reportedly demanding 10,000-ruble ($120) payments for the replacement of documents washed away by the floodwater.[14] Residents of occupied Oleshky found themselves dependent on, and indebted to, the Russian occupation administration to escape from the humanitarian devastation that Russian forces themselves caused by blowing up the KHPP dam.
Russian occupation policies have contributed to a sharp decline in an already-challenging humanitarian situation in the Oleshky area since December 2025.
Oleshky’s location directly on the Dnipro River frontline has exposed its residents to constant drone and artillery strikes, and the co-placement of Russian military personnel and equipment with civilian infrastructure has undoubtedly complicated Ukrainian strike operations against military targets on the left bank.
The Russian occupation administration has continuously refused to take steps to ensure the safety or wellbeing of residents in the face of these military threats, however, and stopped the delivery of food and other critical supplies into Oleshky in late December 2025 by citing the threat of Ukrainian drone strikes.
[15]  Residents reported hunting for food and noted that there were cases of deaths due to starvation, freezing, or lack of medical care as of March 2026.
[16] Ukrainian sources reported that Oleshky’s occupation leadership fled the town for Skadovsk (south of Oleshky, deeper in the rear of occupied Kherson Oblast) in March, abandoning and isolating local residents.
[17] The roads out of Oleshky have become so dangerous due to drone and artillery strikes and unexploded mines, including ordnance that Russian forces reportedly retroactively laid to enforce the effective blockade of the area, that egress from the town is effectively impossible.
[18] Up to three to four thousand civilians, including children, remain within Oleshky itself as of September 2026.
[19] UN and Ukrainian estimates place the population of the wider area around Oleshky and Hola Prystan at 6,000.
[20]
Russia has failed to deliver food, medicine, or other critical goods to the Oleshky area since May 2026. The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine ( HRMMU) published a report on June 25 that found that there had been no food deliveries into Oleshky since May 26.[21] Residents have resorted to eating ground up grains and pasta mixed with baking soda and liquid from expired canned foods, grass, or soup made from garden weeds to survive.[22] An Oleshky resident posted on social media on September 1 that with the end of fruit and vegetable season approaching, people are increasingly “panicky” out of fears that there will be nothing left to eat.[23]
Deaths from starvation or illness are driving a critical sanitary situation in the Oleshky area as residents are unable to bury the bodies of the dead or use the city morgue, which has been completely destroyed.[24] Stray dogs have reportedly become used to the taste of human flesh.[25] Russian officials still had not facilitated food shipment to the Oleshky area as of September 29. Ukrainian Kherson Oblast Head Oleksandr Prokhudin reported on September 27 that units of the Ukrainian National Guard and Marines managed to conduct a covert drone operation to drop four tons of food into Oleshky to ease famine conditions.[26] Prokhudin warned, however, that Russian forces tried to shoot down the drones and are beating residents who were able to collect the delivered aid.
The Kremlin itself has acknowledged it is aware of the situation in the Oleshky area, but has refused to engage in any good-faith efforts to address the situation despite repeated Ukrainian government outreach. Kremlin Spokesperson Dmitry Peskov acknowledged during a press briefing on September 21 that there are challenges with food and medicine supply to occupied Oleshky, but blamed Ukraine entirely for the situation.[27] Alexander “Sasha” Kots, a prominent milblogger who serves on the Kremlin’s Human Rights Council, responded to the situation by similarly blaming Ukraine and called for the opening of a humanitarian corridor to occupied Melitopol (about 200 kilometers east of Oleshky in the rear of Russian-occupied Zaporizhia Oblast).[28] There have been no formal Kremlin offers for a ceasefire to secure a humanitarian corridor out of Oleshky as of the time of writing, however. Ukrainian officials, on the other hand, have made several attempts to negotiate with the Kremlin over the issue of Oleshky:
- First attempt: Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets first raised the issue of a negotiated local humanitarian ceasefire in order to evacuate residents from Oleshky and nearby settlements in May 2026.[29] Lubinets appealed to the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), which stated it was ready to help organize evacuations from the Oleshky area. Lubinets and unspecified Russian counterparts reportedly discussed the situation in Oleshky on May 15, but no agreements arose from these discussions.[30]
- Second attempt goes unanswered: Ukraine’s ceasefire proposals remained unanswered as of July 2026. Lubinets sent another appeal to the ICRC to engage with Russia over the establish

articles.title: Uzbekistan-Belarus trade hits $731.3M in 8M2026 - trend.az
articles.summary: Uzbekistan-Belarus trade hits $731.3M in 8M2026  trend.az
articles.full_text:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 2. Trade turnover between Uzbekistan and Belarus reached $731.3 million in the period from January through August 2026, the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Uzbekistan announced on October 2.
This was reflected in the statement by the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Uzbekistan, following the meeting of the heads of chambers of commerce and industry of the CIS countries held in Minsk today.
According to the information, the meeting was held on the sidelines of the second international industrial exhibition INNOPROM. Belarus brought together Uzbekistan Chamber of Commerce and Industry Chairman Davron Vakhabov, along with heads and representatives of chambers from CIS countries.
The participants discussed expanding trade and economic relations, increasing industrial cooperation, developing joint projects and strengthening direct business ties between entrepreneurs.
Uzbekistan and Belarus have been expanding cooperation across several sectors, with Uzbek-capital projects in Belarus covering livestock, electrical engineering, mechanical engineering, light industry, construction materials, furniture and pharmaceuticals.
In the livestock sector, 39 projects are planned to produce 56,900 head of cattle, with a combined investment value of $107.2 million, according to the Uzbekistan Chamber of Commerce and Industry.
Bilateral trade turnover stood at $965 million in 2025 and reached $731.3 million in the period from January through August 2026, indicating continued expansion in economic ties between the two countries.
"️Davron Vakhabov stressed at the meeting the importance of enriching cooperation between chambers with practical projects, expanding opportunities for entrepreneurs to enter new markets and developing industrial cooperation," the statement said.
Additionally, the meeting addressed greater participation by businesses in international exhibitions and business events, experience sharing, and the development of direct contacts between business representatives from CIS countries.
The participants agreed to continue cooperation on expanding joint business and exhibition events, promoting industrial cooperation and advancing new investment projects.

articles.title: Azerbaijan's deputy prime minister visits Iran: what interests are bringing Baku and Tehran closer? - JAMnews
articles.summary: Azerbaijan's deputy prime minister visits Iran: what interests are bringing Baku and Tehran closer?  JAMnews
articles.full_text:
Azerbaijan’s deputy prime minister visits Iran
At meetings in Tehran attended by Azerbaijani Deputy Prime Minister Shahin Mustafayev, the sides discussed electricity supplies, the development of border infrastructure and transport routes. Iran plans to increase its electricity purchases from Azerbaijan this coming winter. For Baku, meanwhile, the priorities include developing joint energy projects and expanding transit capacity.
However, these talks do not provide grounds to speak of restored political trust. Economic cooperation continues amid tensions stemming from the armed attack on the Azerbaijani embassy in Tehran and a drone incident in Nakhchivan in March this year.
What was discussed in Tehran?
On 29 September, Mustafayev met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. According to the Iranian side, Pezeshkian emphasised the importance of expanding road, air and rail links, as well as implementing agreements reached during talks with ministers.
A statement from the Azerbaijani Cabinet of Ministers also reported meetings with parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei, Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad and Energy Minister Abbas Aliabadi. However, the statement provided no details on the financial terms of the energy projects or specific deadlines for their implementation.
Transport issues featured more prominently during the visit. At a meeting with Iran’s Minister of Roads and Urban Development Farzaneh Sadegh, the sides discussed the capacity of the North-South Corridor, the expansion of the Astara border freight terminal and the Aghband-Kalaleh bridge. According to official information, construction of the bridge has been completed. However, the sides are still discussing the launch of the border-crossing infrastructure. Completing the bridge does not by itself mean that the entire border complex is already operational.
The sides also reviewed progress on agreements reached at the 17th meeting of the joint commission, which took place in Baku in February. This indicates that the September talks also aimed to speed up implementation of previously agreed commitments.
What is known about electricity imports?
According to Trend, citing Iran’s Energy Ministry, TAVANIR electricity company chief Mohammad Allahdad expressed hope on 28 September that Iran could increase electricity imports during the coming colder months. He made the comments at a meeting with Azerbaijani Deputy Energy Minister Elnur Soltanov.
The talks covered direct electricity supplies, the development of joint hydropower plants, and gas and electricity swaps — mechanisms for exchanging the two forms of energy. Allahdad said specialists from the two countries needed to examine the points where their power grids connect and assess their technical capacity before determining possible supply volumes.
The plans announced after the talks do not mean that the sides have already signed an agreement on additional electricity supplies. The published information does not specify supply volumes, prices or start dates. Iran’s intention to increase imports should therefore not be confused with an actual increase in supplies.
According to the Tehran bureau of APA, Soltanov also raised the implementation of the Khudaferin and Ordubad hydropower projects, as well as the participation of private Iranian investors in solar energy projects in Nakhchivan. These initiatives also remain under discussion.
For Azerbaijan, increased electricity exports could provide an additional source of revenue. However, without information on volumes, prices and technical conditions, it is impossible to assess the economic benefits of this cooperation.
The security dimension of the economic talks
The talks in Tehran also covered allegations that Azerbaijan’s territory had been used against Iran. According to Unikal, citing the Mehr news agency, Mustafayev rejected these allegations at a meeting with Mohsen Rezaei.
The fact that the sides raised this issue alongside economic matters shows that security concerns remain relevant.
Relations between the two countries deteriorated sharply after an armed attack on the Azerbaijani embassy in Tehran in January 2023 killed one person. Subsequent contacts helped ease tensions, but a drone incident in Nakhchivan in March 2026 triggered a new crisis.
Azerbaijani officials blamed Iran for the 5 March attack, which damaged an airport and other civilian facilities. Tehran denied any involvement. According to the Azerbaijani Foreign Ministry, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that authorities were investigating the circumstances of the incident. Baku demanded an apology, an explanation and measures to prevent similar incidents in the future.
The suspension of cargo traffic during the crisis showed that a deterioration in security can immediately affect economic ties.
Why does Baku want to avoid further tensions?
In an analysis published on 16 March, Carnegie Endowment researcher Zaur Shiriyev described Baku’s decision to demand an explanation after the drone incident rather than launch a retaliatory strike as an attempt to prevent further escalation.
In his view, Nakhchivan’s vulnerable position was one reason why tensions eased quickly. Transit through Iran plays an important role in the autonomous republic’s land and air connections. Shiriyev also noted that a war in Iran would create risks for Azerbaijan, including a possible influx of refugees and higher prices for imported goods.
This assessment concerns the March crisis. Nevertheless, it helps explain why Azerbaijan seeks to avoid a sharp deterioration in relations with Iran.
The September talks show that Tehran wants to increase electricity imports, while both sides seek to expand cooperation in the energy and transport sectors. These mutual interests provide a basis for continued engagement. However, it would be premature to view the visit as evidence that political mistrust has been overcome.
The outcome of this cooperation will depend on whether the sides can turn their stated intentions into actual supplies, ensure that border crossings operate fully and implement the projects they have outlined.

articles.title: The place of Central Asia in Azerbaijan’s foreign policy - EU Reporter
articles.summary: The place of Central Asia in Azerbaijan’s foreign policy  EU Reporter
articles.full_text:
In recent years, Central Asia has moved from the periphery of Azerbaijan’s foreign policy to become one of its principal geopolitical priorities. This shift cannot be explained solely by the translation of the historical, ethnic, religious, and cultural affinities between Azerbaijan and the states of the region into political relations. The new phase rests on the Caspian Sea’s role as a unifying rather than a dividing geopolitical space, the growing importance of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route-the Middle Corridor-the diversification of energy and digital communications, and the institutionalization of strategic partnerships and alliances between Azerbaijan and the Central Asian states, writes Dr. Matin Mammadli, head of department at the Baku – based Center of Analysis of İnternational Relations and Multiculturalism.
Central Asia’s place in Azerbaijan’s contemporary foreign policy is linked, above all, to the new geopolitical significance of the country’s geographic position. Although geographically located in the South Caucasus, Azerbaijan’s historical and cultural ties, linguistic and civilizational connections, transport infrastructure, energy policy, and position on the Caspian Sea also make it the western link in Central Asia’s political and economic system. In other words, Azerbaijan is more than a South Caucasian state: it is an active participant in a wider geopolitical space where the Caucasus, Central Asia, the Middle East, the Black Sea basin, and Europe intersect.
President Ilham Aliyev has stated that Azerbaijan and the countries of Central Asia form a ‘single historical, cultural, geographical and geopolitical space,’ characterizing the Caspian Sea less as a physical barrier than as a symbol of strategic unity, economic potential, and historical co-operation 1. This perspective reflects a conceptual shift in Azerbaijan’s regional policy: the Caspian is no longer a boundary separating regions but a principal line of communication enabling their economic and political integration. Several interrelated factors determine Central Asia’s importance for Azerbaijan. First, the region gives Azerbaijan strategic depth to the east of the Caspian and access to Asian markets, including China. Second, the growing economic potential of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan makes Azerbaijan a natural partner in their transport, energy, and investment projects. Third, the Central Asian states’ need for alternative export and transit routes enhances the regional importance of Azerbaijan’s port, railway, road, shipping, and energy infrastructure. Fourth, stronger political coordination among the Turkic states expands Azerbaijan’s room for maneuver in the region.
Azerbaijan’s importance to Central Asia is equally fundamental. With no direct access to the world’s oceans, the states of the region need reliable and diversified routes to external markets. In this respect, Azerbaijan is one of the shortest strategic bridges for transporting Central Asian goods toward Europe via the Caspian Sea, the Baku International Sea Trade Port, the Baku–Tbilisi-Kars railway, and Türkiye. Azerbaijan’s existing transport infrastructure also offers Central Asian states alternative routes not only westward but toward Iran, the Persian Gulf, the Black Sea basin, and the Mediterranean. A number of international institutions likewise emphasize that the Middle Corridor is not merely a China-Europe land bridge; it is, first and foremost, an economic mechanism that expands regional trade among Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Georgia, and other corridor countries 2.
This mutual importance has become more apparent since 2022. Disruptions to global supply chains, heightened political and commercial risks associated with traditional northern routes amid the Russia-Ukraine war, rising demand for alternative links between Europe and Asia, and states’ desire to reduce their dependence on particular transport routes have all intensified interest in the Trans-Caspian route. Yet it would be mistaken to regard the Middle Corridor’s significance as merely a temporary consequence of geopolitical crisis. The long-term character of infrastructure projects, growing freight volumes, port expansion, and the development of common tariff arrangements and digital customs mechanisms indicate that the route is gradually becoming a durable regional economic system.
Another important reason for Azerbaijan’s growing attention to Central Asia is the principle of geographic and political diversification in its foreign policy. By developing relations simultaneously with Europe, the United States, Türkiye, Russia, China, the Middle East, and Central Asia, Baku seeks to avoid unilateral dependence on any one center of power. From this perspective, Central Asia is, for Azerbaijan, less an arena of rivalry than a sphere of partnership in which shared interests are reconciled and the principles of sovereignty and mutual benefit prevail. The importance that Azerbaijan and the states of the region attach in their foreign policies to territorial integrity, state sovereignty, non-interference in internal affairs, and multi-vector diplomacy also increases their political compatibility.
The relations emerging between Azerbaijan and Central Asia cannot be adequately explained within the framework of conventional bilateral diplomacy. They involve functional regionalism: the formation of a common sphere of activity through transport, energy, trade, investment, digital communications, and humanitarian ties. This model does not create a supranational political union or constrain states’ sovereignty. Rather, it increases interdependence and resilience while preserving each country’s independent foreign policy. Taken together, relations between Azerbaijan and Central Asia may be characterized by geopolitical and geoeconomic complementarity.
The countries of Central Asia possess energy resources, critical raw materials, agricultural products, industrial goods, and expanding consumer markets. Azerbaijan, in turn, has developed port, shipping, railway, and energy infrastructure capable of facilitating the westward movement of these resources. Central Asia’s production and export potential is thus complemented by Azerbaijan’s transit capacity. For Azerbaijan, the growth of transit freight not only raises port and railway revenues but also creates conditions for the development of warehousing, insurance, customs services, freight forwarding, ship repair, industrial zones, and value-adding processing enterprises.
Azerbaijan’s role for Central Asia is not limited to that of a transit country providing transport services. Baku also serves as a connecting platform for the region’s political and economic relations with Türkiye and Europe. The Azerbaijan-Türkiye alliance, the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars railway, the Southern Gas Corridor, and the emerging green energy route toward the Black Sea provide a multilayered infrastructure base for Central Asia’s westward integration. In this sense, Azerbaijan is more than a geographic passage for Central Asia: it is a strategic gateway to the economic and political space of Türkiye and Europe.
Explaining the rapprochement between Azerbaijan and the Central Asian countries solely in terms of geopolitical and economic interests does not fully capture the nature of their relations. Among the principal foundations of interstate cooperation are the peoples’ shared historical memory, common spiritual values, religious and cultural affinity, and social trust. While material interests make political partnership necessary, cultural and spiritual affinity gives that partnership social legitimacy and longevity.
The peoples of Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan speak languages of the Turkic family and share ethnic and cultural roots, mythological and literary heritage, and similar customs and traditions. This affinity functions as a form of ‘soft infrastructure’ in the development of political relations. Communication in the same or closely related languages, shared historical figures and literary heritage, the Novruz tradition, a connection to Islamic civilization, hospitality, and family values help societies accept cooperation initiatives advanced by their governments.
One of the clearest indications of the importance Azerbaijan attaches to Central Asia is the substantial strengthening in recent years of the treaty and legal basis of its bilateral relations. Azerbaijan has now established relations at the level of strategic partnership or alliance with every state in the region. In addition to ensuring continuity in political dialogue, these documents provide a legal and political framework for cooperation in transport, energy, investment, security, defense, humanitarian affairs, and international organizations. By around mid-2026, Azerbaijan had established alliances with Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Kyrgyzstan, and strategic partnerships with Tajikistan and Turkmenistan. This architecture demonstrates Baku’s transition from episodic diplomacy toward a systematic, long-term regional policy. Although the alliance and strategic partnership documents were signed in different years, their recent activation and supplementation with new mechanisms form part of a coherent regional course.
A new phase in Azerbaijan-Central Asia relations is also associated with Azerbaijan’s inclusion in the format of the Consultative Meetings of the Heads of State of Central Asia. President Ilham Aliyev participated in this format as a guest of honor for the first time in Dushanbe in 2023 and for a second time in Astana in 2024. articles.title: [PRNewswire] IRF Delegation Visits B3 Arch Bridge in Georgia - Yonhap News Agency
articles.summary: [PRNewswire] IRF Delegation Visits B3 Arch Bridge in Georgia  Yonhap News Agency
articles.full_text:
[PRNewswire] IRF Delegation Visits B3 Arch Bridge in Georgia
TBILISI, Georgia Oct. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire=YONHAP/ -- From September 30 to October 2, 2026, the 4th International Road Federation (IRF) Europe and Central Asia Regional Congress was held in Tbilisi, the capital of Georgia. On October 2nd, Roads Department of Georgia led a delegation of congress participants on a special visit to the construction site of the B3 Arch Bridge on the Kvesheti–Kobi section of Georgia's North–South Corridor Highway, undertaken by China Railway 23rd Bureau Group Co., Ltd. The delegation inspected the progress of the project and gained first-hand insight into the capabilities of Chinese enterprises in constructing long-span bridges and implementing standardized project management under the extreme conditions of high-altitude alpine valleys.
The B3 Arch Bridge serves as a key controlling project for the Georgia North-South Corridor Road project. Located in a deep valley of the Caucasus Mountains, the bridge has a total length of 437.875 meters, a main arch net span of 286 meters, and a height difference of 164 meters from the bridge deck to the valley floor. It features a deck-type reinforced concrete separated twin-rib box arch structure, constructed using the cantilever casting method with cable-stayed anchoring. Subjected to extreme environmental challenges—including Beaufort scale 9 strong winds, severe cold down to -20°C, 2-meter-thick snow accumulation, and high-intensity seismic zones—the bridge, upon completion, will become the largest-span reinforced concrete arch bridge in the Caucasus region, with its span ranking among the top worldwide for similar cantilever-cast arch bridges.
During the inspection, the project team of China Railway 23rd Bureau Group delivered a detailed report to the accompanying delegates on core management measures and technical achievements.
These included the implementation of European standards, FIDIC contract management, high-precision closure control for the twin-rib main arch, intelligent monitoring, and wind tunnel test verification.
The delegation closely inspected and inquired about key structural components, such as the main arch ring construction, anchoring system, and cable hoisting system.
They engaged in in-depth exchanges with the Chinese technical team on critical topics, including main arch alignment and stress control, construction procedures, winter construction safety assurance, full-lifecycle maintenance, and follow-up construction organization.
The delegation representative stated that the North-South Corridor Road is one of the most vital transportation infrastructure projects in Georgia's national development strategy, playing a decisive role in strengthening the country's status as an Eurasian transit hub.
As the most technically challenging controlling project along the entire route, the B3 Arch Bridge fully demonstrates the capability of Chinese enterprises in building large-scale bridges under complex geological and extreme climatic conditions.
Strictly adhering to European technical specifications and the FIDIC management system, the project meets world-class standards in quality control, environmental protection, and localized employment, setting a new benchmark for highway and bridge construction in Georgia and across the broader Central Asia–Caucasus region.

Han Shuai, project manager of the China Railway 23rd Bureau Co., Ltd. North–South Corridor Road Project, said that the company would take this visit by the IRF delegation as an opportunity to continue pursuing its overseas business philosophy of "Quality Delivery, Safety First, Standards Alignment and Local Integration." The project team will make every effort to achieve key milestones, including the closure of the B3 main arch in 2026, and develop the project into a model of infrastructure cooperation between China and Georgia and a landmark project for bridge construction in high-altitude mountainous regions under the Belt and Road Initiative.
As a vivid embodiment of the theme of this year's IRF Congress—"Resilient, Intelligent and Safe Roads Driving Sustainable Growth"—the site visit to the B3 Arch Bridge brought delegates from conference halls to the front lines of project construction, transforming conceptual discussions into first-hand evidence from an actual engineering project. The bridge spans not only the deep valleys of the Caucasus, but also represents a new level of mutual trust and cooperation between China, Europe and Central Asia in the field of transportation infrastructure.
Source: China Railway 23rd Bureau Group Co., Ltd.

articles.title: How Donald Trump’s Belarus Potash Deal Gives Russia Another Ace To Play - nationalinterest.org
articles.summary: How Donald Trump’s Belarus Potash Deal Gives Russia Another Ace To Play  nationalinterest.org
articles.full_text:
Shipping Belarus’ potash to the United States would undermine US-Canada trade and give Russia a chokehold on US agriculture.
President Donald Trump announced on Truth Social on September 21 that his administration was negotiating a “massive” deal to buy potash from Belarus, claiming farmers would pay substantially less than they do for the Canadian supply. Potash, a potassium-rich mineral, is one of the three core nutrients (alongside nitrogen and phosphorus) that fertilize American crops, and most US farmers get it from Canada.
The next day, the president walked it back, partly. In follow-up remarks, he said the United States will keep buying Canadian potash but will still pursue the Belarus deal: “Belarus has a lot of potash, and our farmers need good prices, and we want to get a lower price.” So Canada stays in the picture for now, and Minsk becomes a bargaining chip. Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe shot back, calling it “blood potash” and noting that Belarusian potash must cross Russia, an ocean, and half the continental United States to reach a Midwest farm.
Obviously, the premier of Canada’s potash-producing province would be cross with the deal, but American farmers should be wary, too.
Start with the president’s cost claim, because it doesn’t hold up. Belarus is landlocked, and EU sanctions have closed its most direct export route: the Lithuanian port of Klaipeda. With that door shut, every tonne bound for the US must travel overland through Russia, load at a Russian port, and cross the Atlantic before touching American soil.
Canadian potash, by contrast, moves from Saskatchewan over an established rail and port network with direct lines into the American Midwest. It’s a supply chain decades in the making, with no war zone anywhere on the route. Fertilizer analyst Josh Linville put it plainly: even if a route through EU states to the Baltic were possible, “the relatively low current value of potash makes it hard to justify exports through the Baltic and across the Atlantic.” The White House’s math doesn’t add up on paper, let alone in practice.
But set aside the cost question, and this is where the prospect of Belarusian potash becomes a geopolitical nightmare. The EU sanctions blocking a route through the European Union aren’t going anywhere, and repealing them would require unanimous consent from all 27 EU member states. This just is not going to happen without political change in Belarus. Belarusian potash exports are thus permanently dependent on Russian rail and ports to reach any market.
That means American farmers’ access to a critical input for the planting season would run through infrastructure that Russian President Vladimir Putin controls. He could end that export supply chain with a phone call.
By going this route, the Trump administration would hand President Putin an ace he could play at any time as leverage over the US economy and the food supply. This could, if the deal is as “massive” as the president says it is, mirror European dependence on Russian natural gas. Handing Putin that second lever of pressure on the West, now over the fertilizer that feeds American crops, represents a self-inflicted vulnerability with a foreign policy price tag that nobody has yet priced in.
Supporters of the deal will say that Trump is just playing hardball to bring down costs for farmers after years of high input prices. That instinct—wanting cheaper fertilizer—is entirely reasonable. But the evidence suggests that sourcing it through a landlocked, sanctioned country won’t deliver. America would be reliant on Putin’s goodwill.
The Trump administration already ran this experiment once, and the results should have settled the question. When Washington imposed 50 percent tariffs on Canadian aluminum, Canadian producers didn’t sit on their hands. Aluminerie Alouette, North America’s largest smelter, boosted its European sales from 4 percent to 57 percent in mere months.
In response, the United States leaned harder on suppliers in the Persian Gulf, with the UAE and Bahrain together supplying a quarter of unwrought aluminum imports. Then the Iran War and disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz forced American manufacturers to realize that their new supply sat on the wrong side of a contested waterway. Punishing a reliable neighbor to chase savings from a geopolitically exposed alternative proved a mistake, one the administration shouldn’t repeat, especially because Canadian producers can look elsewhere.
Canada, while economically reliant on the United States, is not necessarily a captive supplier that the trade fight assumes. Roughly half of Canada’s potash exports go to buyers outside the US, which proves Canadian producers do, in fact, have options elsewhere when it makes sense. Pushing American farmers away from that supply doesn’t risk a worse deal between Canada and the United States—it risks no deal at all—if Ottawa decides diversification should run further than it already has.
Of course, there is a better path forward: fix the trading relationship with Canada, a neighbor unburdened by war, and a reliable supplier with advanced infrastructure. Don’t chase imaginary savings that depend on Vladimir Putin’s good graces to keep the supply chain functional.
American farmers need affordable fertilizer, but cheap inputs aren’t cheap if one cost is betting that Moscow won’t cut off supply halfway through planting season.
About the Author: David Clement
David Clement is the policy director at the Consumer Choice Center. David holds a BA in Political Science and an MA in International Relations from Wilfrid Laurier University. Previously, David worked as a research assistant to the Canada Research Chair in International Human Rights. David has been featured regularly on the CBC, Global News, The Toronto Star, and other major Canadian news outlets.

articles.title: Pashinyan says TRIPP will link Azerbaijan and Armenia by rail - Operativ Məlumat Mərkəzi
articles.summary: Pashinyan says TRIPP will link Azerbaijan and Armenia by rail  Operativ Məlumat Mərkəzi
articles.full_text:
Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said the TRIPP project would establish a direct railway link between Azerbaijan and Armenia. He made the remarks on Friday via video address to a meeting of the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council in Minsk, the capital of Belarus.
The meeting was attended by the prime ministers of Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, all members of the Eurasian Economic Union.
TRIPP could expand regional rail links
Pashinyan said Armenia continues to promote its “Crossroads of Peace” initiative, which aims to expand transport, energy and digital connectivity in the region. He said one of its key elements is the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity, or TRIPP.
“The TRIPP project will establish a direct railway link between Armenia and Azerbaijan,” Pashinyan said. He added that it could integrate Armenia into the international railway network and help create a rail connection between the Persian Gulf and the Black Sea.
The prime minister said the development would be significant for Azerbaijan, Armenia, Georgia and Iran. Pashinyan said he had briefed his counterparts during closed-door discussions on efforts to open regional transport infrastructure following the establishment of peace between Azerbaijan and Armenia.
He said Yerevan was awaiting measures to improve the efficiency of Armenia’s railway network. Pashinyan did not provide further details.
Barriers within the Eurasian Economic Union
TRIPP aims to provide a transport link through Armenia between Azerbaijan’s mainland and the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic, while also supporting broader regional connectivity. The project is considered one of the main avenues for developing economic and transport ties between Azerbaijan and Armenia.
The foreign ministers of the two countries met in New York on Sept. 24 on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly session and discussed the development of transport and economic ties.
In his address, Pashinyan also voiced concern about restrictions within the Eurasian Economic Union. He said administrative barriers were hindering the effective functioning of the union’s single market.
The prime minister said there had been no significant progress on a number of outstanding issues since the previous meeting, held in August in Cholpon-Ata, Kyrgyzstan. “In particular, restrictions and administrative barriers that seriously impede the full and effective functioning of the single market remain in place,” Pashinyan said.
He called for continued dialogue to resolve difficulties obstructing the export and transit of Armenian goods, in line with the Eurasian Economic Union’s rules. Pashinyan stressed the importance of the free movement of goods, services, capital and labor, as well as food security and stable supplies of agricultural products, for the single market.
In his view, greater progress in removing trade barriers could create stable trade flows and predictable conditions for businesses in Eurasian Economic Union member states.

articles.title: Uzbekistan, Oman move to expand trade, investment, and transport co-op - trend.az
articles.summary: Uzbekistan, Oman move to expand trade, investment, and transport co-op  trend.az
articles.full_text:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 2. Uzbekistan and Oman discussed prospects for expanding bilateral trade and investment, strengthening industrial cooperation, and enhancing transport connectivity during a visit to Muscat by a delegation led by Minister of Investment, Industry and Trade Laziz Kudratov from September 30 to October 2.
This was reflected in the statement by the Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade of Uzbekistan.
According to the Ministry, in the course of the meeting, Kudratov held talks with Oman’s Minister of Economy Khamis bin Saif Al Jabri and Minister of Commerce, Industry and Investment Promotion Anwar bin Hilal Al Jabri. The sides reviewed opportunities to increase trade and investment, develop industrial cooperation and strengthen transport and logistics corridors.
“Uzbekistan is interested in expanding economic cooperation with Oman across trade, investment, industry, energy and logistics, while creating new opportunities for businesses from both countries,” the Uzbek side said.
The Uzbek delegation also held meetings with Omani companies operating in logistics, energy, petrochemicals, electrical engineering, mining, banking and tourism. Discussions covered the development of new production and logistics facilities, export routes, energy storage systems, data centers, raw-material processing and direct supplies.
Particular attention was given to strengthening the legal framework for bilateral economic ties. The sides agreed to work on preferential trade and investment protection agreements, as well as cooperation on transport corridors and joint investment projects.
Moreover, Uzbekistan and Oman plan to organize a business forum, an exhibition showcasing Uzbekistan’s investment and economic potential, and meetings between major companies from the two countries.
The agreements reached during the visit are expected to provide a framework for expanding private-sector ties and developing new investment and trade projects across multiple sectors.

articles.title: Uzbekistan, Denmark establish bilateral commission on trade, investment - trend.az
articles.summary: Uzbekistan, Denmark establish bilateral commission on trade, investment  trend.az
articles.full_text:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 3. Uzbekistan and Denmark agreed to establish a bilateral commission on trade, economic and investment cooperation in Tashkent on Oct. 2.
This was reflected in the statement by the Uzbekistan's Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade.
The agreement was reached during the Uzbekistan-Denmark Business Roundtable in Tashkent on Oct. 2, attended by Uzbekistan’s Minister of Investment, Industry and Trade Laziz Kudratov and Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen.
The Uzbek delegation was headed by Deputy Prime Minister Jamshid Khodjaev, while the Danish delegation was led by Rasmussen.
The sides discussed expanding cooperation in industry, transport and logistics, energy, water management and agriculture, digitalization and financing. Particular attention was given to equipment localization, terminal infrastructure, renewable energy, energy efficiency and modernization of water supply systems.
Representatives of the Export and Investment Fund of Denmark (EIFO) and Danish companies, including FLSmidth, Grundfos, Maersk, AVK International, Scan Global Logistics, Carlsberg and ByteAll Energy, participated in the discussions.
The business program also included B2B and B2G meetings focused on developing joint initiatives and identifying opportunities for cooperation between companies and government institutions.
As a result of the talks, Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade and Denmark’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs signed a memorandum on establishing a bilateral commission on trade, economic and investment cooperation.
The new mechanism is expected to provide an institutional platform for developing trade and investment ties, coordinating joint initiatives and identifying new opportunities for cooperation between Uzbek and Danish businesses.

articles.title: Kazakhstan, Denmark seek to deepen trade, investment cooperation - Qazinform
articles.summary: Kazakhstan, Denmark seek to deepen trade, investment cooperation  Qazinform
articles.full_text:
Kazakhstan and Denmark agreed to strengthen trade, investment and transport cooperation during talks between their foreign ministers, highlighting growing economic ties and new opportunities for collaboration, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Kazakh Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi met with Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen, who had arrived in Kazakhstan on an official visit, to discuss bilateral relations and regional and international issues.
The ministers focused on expanding trade and economic cooperation, noting continued growth in trade turnover and foreign direct investment between the two countries. Bilateral trade reached $163 million in 2025, while cumulative Danish direct investment in Kazakhstan since 2005 exceeded $394 million.
A key topic was a major investment project by Carlsberg Group, which built a PepsiCo soft drinks production plant in the Ili district of Kazakhstan's Almaty region. Rasmussen attended the facility's opening ceremony on Oct. 1.
With investment totaling $344 million, the plant is expected to become one of Carlsberg's largest production sites globally, with annual production capacity of up to 1 billion litres and the creation of 230 jobs.
The sides also discussed cooperation on the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, also known as the Middle Corridor, and its role in strengthening transport links between Europe and Asia. Particular attention was given to potential cooperation with Danish shipping company Maersk to boost cargo flows along the route.
"Denmark is an important partner for us in Northern Europe. We attach great importance to the development of our bilateral relations and seek to give greater substance to our trade and economic cooperation through concrete and significant projects," Tileuberdi said.
Rasmussen reaffirmed Denmark's interest in expanding ties with Kazakhstan, citing the growing strategic importance of Central Asia in Denmark's foreign policy and economic agenda. He also highlighted the appointment of Lars Thuesen as Denmark's ambassador to Kazakhstan and special representative of the Danish Foreign Ministry for Central Asia.
The ministers exchanged views on regional and international developments, cooperation within the United Nations and other multilateral organizations, and prospects for strengthening ties between Central Asia and Northern Europe.
Rasmussen also led a high-level Danish business delegation at the Kazakh-Danish Business Forum in Konaev, where companies from both countries discussed investment opportunities and joint projects in priority sectors of Kazakhstan's economy.
Following the talks, the two sides signed several memorandums of understanding, including a memorandum of understanding on the establishment of a bilateral commission on trade, economic and investment cooperation between the foreign ministries of Kazakhstan and Denmark.
Earlier, it was reported that the Danish Foreign Minister's visit comes ahead of the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Kazakhstan and Denmark, which will be celebrated next year. In Astana, Rasmussen is set to meet President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.

articles.full_text:

The agreements were reached during a September 30–October 2 working visit by Uzbekistan’s Minister of Investment, Industry and Trade Laziz Kudratov, who held meetings with Omani government officials and business representatives.
Kudratov held talks with Oman’s Minister of Economy Khamis bin Saif Al Jabri and Minister of Commerce, Industry and Investment Promotion Anwar bin Hilal Al Jabri. The sides discussed bilateral trade and investment, industrial cooperation, transport and logistics corridors and other areas of economic cooperation.
Meetings with Omani businesses covered logistics, energy, petrochemicals, electrical engineering, mining, banking and tourism. The parties considered new production and logistics capacities, export routes, energy storage systems, data centres, raw-material processing and direct supplies.

articles.title: IFC Identifies Three Sectors With Investment Potential in Uzbekistan - uzdaily.uz
articles.summary: IFC Identifies Three Sectors With Investment Potential in Uzbekistan  uzdaily.uz
articles.full_text:
Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — Logistics, tourism and pharmaceuticals have significant potential to attract private investment in Uzbekistan, according to the International Finance Corporation (IFC).
With the necessary reforms, the sectors could attract billions of dollars in capital and contribute to the creation of hundreds of thousands of jobs.
The findings were outlined in an article by Lisa Kaestner, IFC Division Director for Türkiye, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, published on 29 September 2026. The article presents findings from the World Bank Group’s Country Private Sector Diagnostic (CPSD) for Uzbekistan.
According to Kaestner, Uzbekistan has made significant progress in economic reforms over the past eight years. The CPSD identifies sectors where private capital could play a substantial role while addressing remaining regulatory and infrastructure constraints.
In logistics, the potential is linked primarily to Uzbekistan’s geographical position along the emerging Middle Corridor between China and Europe. With the necessary reforms, the sector could attract around US$1 billion in private investment and create approximately 100,000 direct and indirect jobs by 2030.
A major constraint remains the shortage of modern warehouse infrastructure. Uzbekistan has 513,000 square meters of certified Class A warehouse space, compared with estimated demand of 4.1 million square meters. Logistics costs are also 15–25% higher than on leading Eurasian routes.
The article says attracting investors will require more transparent land allocation rules, improved permitting procedures, digital systems and logistics infrastructure.
In tourism, the number of foreign and other tourist arrivals increased from 1 million in 2016 to 11.7 million in 2025.
The government aims to raise this figure to 20 million by 2030.
However, according to the analysis, further development of the sector requires a shift from focusing solely on the number of tourists toward increasing the economic returns generated by each tourism product. Standardized land-lease rules, secure usage rights and professional management of tourism facilities could support the development of hotels, adaptive reuse projects for historic buildings, as well as nature and adventure tourism.
Private investment potential in tourism is estimated at up to US$4.2 billion by 2030. The sector is also expected to create up to 180,000 direct and indirect jobs.
Pharmaceuticals represent another area of opportunity. Uzbekistan’s pharmaceutical market is estimated at around US$2 billion, with more than 85% of products supplied through imports.
By harmonizing quality standards and regulations with international requirements, Uzbekistan could expand domestic production and increase the sector’s export potential. Estimated investment potential stands at US$108–189 million.
The development of pharmaceutical manufacturing is expected to create between 11,700 and 20,400 highly skilled jobs.
Measures identified in the article include developing bioequivalence research, improving Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standards and requirements for active pharmaceutical ingredients, and strengthening the national testing system.
Further priorities include digitalizing registration and serialization processes, harmonizing standards and strengthening enforcement.
Kaestner noted that the three sectors do not exhaust Uzbekistan’s investment potential. A common condition for their development is an industry and broader economic environment in which private companies can invest, compete, expand and enter foreign markets.
According to the article, the World Bank Group is ready to support Uzbekistan in implementing measures to remove barriers to private investment and developing markets that create conditions for investors and the country’s economy.

articles.full_text:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 3. Uzbekistan and Denmark are seeking to expand bilateral trade after the value of trade turnover between the two countries increased nearly fivefold in recent years, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev said during a meeting with Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen in Tashkent on Oct. 2.
This was reflected in the statement by the press service of the Uzbek president.
The sides discussed practical steps to expand cooperation in the political, trade, economic and cultural-humanitarian spheres, with particular attention to increasing mutual trade and attracting Danish investment, technologies and expertise to Uzbekistan.
“Over the past years, trade turnover has increased almost fivefold,” Mirziyoyev said, according to the Uzbek president’s office.
The Uzbek president highlighted opportunities to further develop cooperation with Danish companies in energy, pharmaceuticals, transport and logistics, agriculture and other sectors. Danish companies are already involved in joint projects in Uzbekistan covering mining, chemicals, food production, agriculture and water supply.
The meeting also addressed education, culture and tourism, as well as current international and regional issues.
The parties agreed to further strengthen the institutional and legal framework for systematically expanding Uzbekistan-Denmark cooperation.
Uzbekistan-Denmark relations have gained momentum in recent years, with cooperation expanding across political, trade, investment and sectoral areas. Uzbekistan appointed its first ambassador to Denmark, with residence in Stockholm, in 2025, while Denmark appointed a special representative for Central Asia in 2026. Bilateral trade has increased nearly fivefold in recent years, while Danish companies are involved in projects in Uzbekistan covering mining, chemicals, food production, agriculture and water supply. The two sides are also exploring opportunities in energy, pharmaceuticals, transport and logistics, the agro-industrial sector, and other areas.

articles.title: Central Asian Nations Reframe Afghanistan as Economic Opportunity - TOLOnews
articles.summary: Central Asian Nations Reframe Afghanistan as Economic Opportunity  TOLOnews
articles.full_text:
Representatives of Central Asian countries announced on the sidelines of the extraordinary meeting of the Regional Contact Group in Astana that they are working to develop a joint strategy regarding Afghanistan and no longer view the country as a threat, but rather as an opportunity for access to South Asian markets.
Yerkin Tokumov, Kazakhstan’s Special Representative for Afghanistan, said his country’s perspective toward Afghanistan has changed and, despite not recognizing the Islamic Emirate, Astana has continued its trade, economic, and humanitarian cooperation.
Economic analyst Mohammad Nabi Afghan added: “Central Asian countries need Afghanistan’s geographic position and now, in many sectors, they practically want to engage, including in infrastructure connectivity with South Asia, or accessing the Middle East through Afghanistan, as they increasingly need to connect to this region.”
Ismatullah Ergashev, Uzbekistan’s representative for Afghanistan, also said that Central Asian countries may soon begin implementing joint projects in Afghanistan and described the country as a land bridge between Central and South Asia.
Referring to growing economic interactions, he added that Uzbekistan’s trade volume with Afghanistan reached nearly $1.7 billion last year and emphasized that Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan have, through these projects, turned Afghanistan into one of their key trading partners.
Businessman Omid Haidari said: “Central Asian countries, especially Uzbekistan, are good alternative partners for our exports and imports, and we are confident that the Islamic Emirate has also made significant efforts in this regard.”
Meanwhile, the Ministry of Economy announced that Afghanistan’s ties with Central Asian countries are expanding.
The ministry stressed that strengthening cooperation with countries in this region can provide mutual benefits for Afghanistan and Central Asia.
Abdul Latif Nazari, Deputy Minister of Economy, said: “Afghanistan’s relations with Central Asian countries are expanding, and these countries can have comprehensive cooperation with Afghanistan in the fields of transport, trade, industry, and agriculture, and this cooperation can ensure the interests of Afghanistan and Central Asian countries.”
At the meeting, attended by representatives of Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan, trade, economic relations, transit issues, and coordination of regional approaches toward Afghanistan were at the top of the agenda.
